theme: Solomon’s reign; the kingdom divides; Rehoboam
readingInstruction: Read 2 Chronicles 8:1-12:16. Solomon’s reign ends, the kingdom divides, and Rehoboam, humbled by Shishak’s invasion, repents for a moment. Read for the Chronicler’s pattern: seek the LORD and prosper; forsake him and suffer.
settingTheScene: The Chronicler gives Solomon’s reign a glowing finish, with the visit of the queen of Sheba, and omits his sin with foreign wives. He wants his readers to remember the golden age. Then the story turns on Rehoboam, who rejects wise counsel, and the northern tribes break away. From this point, the Chronicler largely follows the kings of Judah, the line of David, and ignores the northern kingdom except where it touches Judah.
observation: “And the queen of Sheba said, The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom” (9:5).
“Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne” (9:8).
“But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him” (10:8).
“So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day” (10:19).
“The priests and Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places” (11:13).
“And those who set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel” (11:16).
“When Rehoboam had established his kingdom and was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him” (12:1).
“And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction” (12:12).
interpretation:
The Chronicler gives the pattern that will recur in every reign. The king and the people either seek the LORD or abandon him, and the results follow. Solomon’s wisdom draws the queen of Sheba from afar. She marvels, and she blesses the LORD. The glory of Solomon’s reign points beyond itself.

Rehoboam shows the reverse. He asks for advice from the elders, who counsel gentleness, and from his young friends, who counsel harshness. He chooses the young men’s counsel and answers the people roughly. The kingdom splits. Notice that the Chronicler says it was “a turn of affairs brought about by God,” to fulfill his word. Even human folly is under God’s rule.

The Levites and priests leave the north, and many from all the tribes who “set their hearts to seek the LORD” come to Jerusalem. This is a key idea: the true Israel was where God’s worship was. Jeroboam had appointed his own priests for the high places and golden calves. The faithful choose to follow God and leave their land and property behind.

When Rehoboam is established and strong, he forsakes the law, and Egypt’s Shishak comes up against Jerusalem. A prophet explains: “You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you.” The leaders humble themselves, saying, “The LORD is righteous.” God relents in part. Judah will serve Shishak “that they may know the difference between serving me and serving the kings of the countries.” The chapter ends with a verdict: Rehoboam “did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.”

Contrast this with Ezra, who “set his heart to study the law.” The heart is the central matter.
connection: Matthew 12:42 says the queen of the South will rise at the judgment, “for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” Proverbs 11:14: in an abundance of counselors there is safety. James 4:6: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Hebrews 11:25 notes Moses choosing to share ill-treatment with God’s people. 1 Kings 12 records the split.
application:
Ask where you are tempted to take the advice that is easy instead of the advice that is wise. Seek counsel from someone older and wiser.

Notice the “set your heart to seek the LORD” language and ask whether your heart is set.

When you fail, remember Rehoboam’s brief humbling and God’s mercy.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to set your heart to seek him.
Ask him to give you humility to listen to wise counsel.
Ask him to help you return when you fail.
